name: Ankle fracture (malleolar) and syndesmosis injury

classifications.name: Danis-Weber
classifications.summary: Level of the fibular fracture relative to the syndesmosis: A below (syndesmosis intact), B at the level (syndesmosis variably injured), C above (syndesmosis disrupted)

classifications.name: Lauge-Hansen
classifications.summary: Mechanism-based: foot position (supination or pronation) plus deforming force (adduction, abduction, external rotation); supination-external rotation is the most common pattern and is staged I-IV by the sequence of structures that fail

classifications.name: AO/OTA 44
classifications.summary: Malleolar segment; 44A infrasyndesmotic, 44B transsyndesmotic, 44C suprasyndesmotic, each subdivided by medial-side and posterior-malleolar involvement

why_biologic: Mostly a hardware procedure (plates, screws, fibular nails, syndesmotic screws or suture-button devices); biologics enter only at the margins: injectable calcium-phosphate cement to augment screw purchase in osteoporotic metaphyseal bone or to fill an impaction void in posterior-malleolar or pilon-type extension, DBM or BMAC at a medial malleolar or fibular nonunion, and antibiotic-eluting carriers in open fractures. The syndesmosis itself is a ligament repair with no accepted bone-biologic role.
autograft_standard: Acute fixation rarely uses graft. For malleolar nonunion the standard is revision fixation with local or iliac-crest cancellous autograft; iliac harvest carries donor-site pain and a second incision in a largely outpatient population.
volume_note: NEISS (US emergency departments) estimated 673,214 ankle fractures over 2012-2016, about 135,000 per year, incidence 4.22 per 10,000 person-years, 16.0% admitted (Scheer 2020, PMID 32354504). In adults 65+ NEISS estimated 241,449 ankle fractures over 2016-2023 with incidence rising from 49.1 to 63.0 per 100,000 (PMID 41616724). These are ED-presenting counts, not operative counts; no US ORIF volume was found.
challenge: Volume is now sourced to NEISS (ED-presenting, not operative). Nonunion remains unpooled: no meta-analysis reports an overall ankle-fracture nonunion rate; only diabetic and nicotine-stratified cohorts were found (searched 2026-10-22). Biologics are not routine in malleolar fixation and the record should not imply otherwise.
nonunion_note: No pooled ankle-fracture nonunion figure exists in a meta-analysis: PubMed '(ankle fracture OR malleolar) AND nonunion AND (systematic review OR meta-analysis)' returned 19 records, none pooling nonunion after ORIF. Cohort data: Lavery 2020 (n=439, nonunion defined as not healed at 6 months) found diabetes OR 6.5 for nonunion (PMID 32600558) and a diabetic-only cohort (n=139) had 24.5% nonunion (PMID 36251594); a TriNetX bimalleolar-ORIF cohort (8,882 matched pairs) reported nonunion RR 1.65 at 2 years with smoked nicotine (PMID 41441890). Rates in non-diabetic, non-smoking patients are low single digits in these series.

name: Tibiotalar (ankle) arthrodesis, open or arthroscopic
why_biologic: Autograft or a substitute is packed into the prepared joint to bridge gaps and, in high-risk hosts (smokers, diabetics, prior triple fusion, osteonecrosis, revision), to add osteoinductive or osteogenic signal. Augment (rhPDGF-BB/beta-TCP) is the only product with an FDA label for this use. A 2026 series of 227 CT-verified fusions found no difference with or without graft (92.4% vs 92.8%), supporting selective rather than routine use.
autograft_standard: Local bone from joint preparation, with iliac-crest, proximal-tibial, or calcaneal cancellous autograft for defects; iliac harvest adds donor-site pain, which the Augment pivotal trial used as its principal clinical argument.
volume_note: Nationwide Inpatient Sample 2016-2019 identified 12,325 inpatient ankle arthrodeses, about 3,100 per year, inpatient only (PMID 39931642). Medicare FFS: 19,120 ankle arthrodeses vs 9,059 total ankle replacements in the study window, with annual AA falling from 2,080 (2005) to 1,823 (2014) (PMID 32830583). All foot-and-ankle arthrodeses rose from 8.2 to 20.2 per 100,000 between 1994 and 2006 in NSAS/NHDS data (PMID 26213159). No all-payer, all-setting US count exists; outpatient/ASC cases are not in NIS.
challenge: Pooled nonunion for screw-fixed ankle arthrodesis is about 4% (Izzo 2023), well below the historical 10-15%; quoting the higher figure invites challenge. Volume figures are inpatient (NIS) or Medicare-only; there is no all-payer count that includes ASC cases.
nonunion_note: Proportional meta-analysis of 38 studies/1,990 ankles fixed with screws: pooled fusion 96% (95% CI 95-98), i.e. about 4% nonunion; complications 15%, reoperation excluding hardware removal 3% (Izzo 2023, PMID 36795152). Older figures: 9% revision with nonunion 65% of revisions (PMID 17768184), 7.7% nonunion in 284 arthroscopic cases (PMID 37212175), 6.1% for single-joint foot/ankle fusions in an umbrella meta-analysis (PMID 35705455).

name: Diabetic foot osteomyelitis and calcaneal osteomyelitis: dead-space management after debridement

classifications.name: Cierny-Mader
classifications.summary: Anatomic type I medullary, II superficial, III localized, IV diffuse; host class A healthy, B compromised (local, systemic or both), C treatment worse than disease

classifications.name: IWGDF/IDSA infection severity
classifications.summary: Grade 1 uninfected, 2 mild (skin only), 3 moderate (deeper or larger), 4 severe (systemic signs); osteomyelitis flagged with an O suffix in the 2023 IWGDF/IDSA classification

why_biologic: After resection of infected bone the cavity must be filled to avoid hematoma and recurrence; resorbable calcium-sulfate or calcium-sulfate/hydroxyapatite carriers deliver local antibiotic at concentrations systemic therapy cannot reach and resorb without a second procedure. Cerament G is the only US-authorized antibiotic-eluting void filler; surgeon-mixed Stimulan beads are widespread but off-label for the antibiotic. The strongest data are from long-bone osteomyelitis (96% eradication at one procedure in 100 patients; 94% infection-free at 6 years), while diabetic-foot-specific series are small and mixed (42% recurrence in one 45-case US calcium-sulfate series; no benefit in a 25-patient Greek comparison).
autograft_standard: No autograft standard; the comparator is debridement plus systemic antibiotics with the cavity left open, packed, or managed with PMMA beads that need removal.
volume_note: No verified US count for diabetic foot osteomyelitis admissions found in this sweep.
challenge: No US annual count for diabetic foot osteomyelitis admissions or resections was found. Searched PubMed 2026-10-22: '(diabetic foot osteomyelitis[Title]) AND (United States OR national OR nationwide) AND (incidence OR epidemiology OR trends OR burden OR hospitalizations)' returned no US national count; HCUP/NIS diabetic-foot amputation counts exist but do not isolate osteomyelitis dead-space management. Flag retained.

name: Foot and ankle nonunion and high-risk revision fusion (general)

classifications.name: Weber-Cech
classifications.summary: Hypertrophic (viable, mechanically unstable), oligotrophic, atrophic (biologically inert); infected nonunion is managed as a separate category

why_biologic: Across foot and ankle fusions the pooled nonunion prevalence is 8.1% (6.1% for single joints, 27.1% for TTC). Revision for atrophic nonunion needs osteoinduction and osteogenic cells beyond what the bed provides, so BMAC, DBM, cellular allograft, rhPDGF-BB (on-label only for primary hindfoot/ankle fusion), and off-label rhBMP-2 are stacked onto revised fixation. A 2025 review concludes BMAC has moderate-to-high evidence for percutaneous treatment of delayed union and nonunion but that systematic reviews question its benefit in arthrodesis.
autograft_standard: Iliac-crest cancellous autograft remains the reference for atrophic nonunion; it is limited by volume and donor-site pain, and many foot/ankle patients are smokers or diabetics in whom harvest morbidity is higher.
volume_note: Derived rather than counted: 8.1% of all foot/ankle fusions (PMID 35705455); no US nonunion count found.
challenge: Volume is derived (8.1% of foot/ankle fusions, PMID 35705455), not counted. Searched PubMed 2026-10-22 for US nonunion counts (foot/ankle nonunion AND United States/national AND incidence/trends): none found. Flag retained; the derived figure is the best available.

name: First metatarsophalangeal joint arthrodesis (hallux rigidus, severe hallux valgus, failed implant salvage)

classifications.name: Coughlin-Shurnas (hallux rigidus)
classifications.summary: Grade 0 stiffness only; 1 mild osteophytes; 2 moderate joint narrowing; 3 severe narrowing with cysts, pain at end range; 4 grade 3 plus mid-range pain

why_biologic: Primary fusion needs little or no graft and nonunion is 5-9%; salvage after a failed silicone or metallic implant leaves a shortening defect that requires a structural interposition graft (iliac autograft or allograft block) and carries a 16.5% pooled nonunion. Biologic use is therefore concentrated in revision and salvage, not primary cases.
autograft_standard: Local bone for primary; iliac-crest tricortical autograft for interposition in salvage, with donor-site morbidity driving use of allograft blocks.
volume_note: No US annual count found. NSAS/NHDS data put all foot-and-ankle arthrodeses at 20.2 per 100,000 in 2006 (PMID 26213159) without a first-MTP breakout. A 2026 PearlDiver national claims study of primary vs revision first-MTP arthrodesis (2,099 matched pairs) reports 2-year nonunion diagnoses of 4.1% after primary and 9.9% after revision/salvage fusion, repeat fusion 4.4% vs 7.2% (PMID 42602317); the study does not report a national annual volume.
nonunion_note: Claims-coded nonunion diagnosis at 2 years: 4.1% primary vs 9.9% revision/salvage first-MTP arthrodesis (PearlDiver, PMID 42602317).
challenge: No national annual count for first-MTP arthrodesis was found (searched PubMed 2026-10-22 for first metatarsophalangeal/hallux AND United States/national AND incidence/volume/utilization; the only national database study, PMID 42602317, reports matched cohorts, not totals). Flag retained for volume.

name: Hallux valgus correction: distal/shaft osteotomy and Lapidus (first TMT) arthrodesis
why_biologic: A minor biologic use. Chevron and scarf osteotomies heal reliably without graft. Lapidus arthrodesis nonunion ranges from 0.7% (plantar plating) to 5.3% (screws only) in a 1,176-patient meta-analysis, so some surgeons add DBM, BMAC, or a small cellular allograft, and opening-wedge medial-cuneiform (Cotton) osteotomies use a structural wedge (allograft, bioactive glass, titanium, or porous PEEK). Treace Medical's Lapiplasty system is the volume driver in this segment.
autograft_standard: Local bone from joint preparation; a Cotton wedge historically used iliac-crest tricortical autograft, now largely replaced by allograft or synthetic wedges.
volume_note: No verified all-payer US count. CMS Medicare Part B data 2013-2022 show a substantial decline in bunionectomies in Medicare beneficiaries with a rising share of Lapidus procedures (PMID 40154771; counts are in the paper, not the abstract). Hallux valgus surgery is overwhelmingly outpatient/ASC and so is invisible to NIS.
challenge: Searched PubMed 2026-10-22 (hallux valgus/bunion/Lapidus AND United States/national AND incidence/trends/volume): only the Medicare-only trend paper (PMID 40154771) is US; the annual counts are in its tables, not retrieved here. Flag retained.

name: Proximal fifth metatarsal (Jones, zone II-III) fracture and nonunion

classifications.name: Lawrence-Botte zones
classifications.summary: Zone 1 tuberosity avulsion; zone 2 metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction (the true Jones fracture, watershed blood supply); zone 3 proximal diaphyseal stress fracture

classifications.name: Torg
classifications.summary: Diaphyseal stress fractures: I acute (sharp margins, no intramedullary sclerosis), II delayed union (widened line, intramedullary sclerosis), III nonunion (sclerotic obliteration of the canal)

why_biologic: Intramedullary screw fixation is the standard in athletes; the watershed blood supply drives delayed union, nonunion and refracture, so surgeons add BMAC, DBM, or calcaneal autograft at the fracture site. A 2022 meta-analysis of 718 athlete fractures found union of 98.5% with orthobiologic augmentation versus 93.8% with fixation alone, with no comparative trials. Revision for nonunion or refracture uses a larger screw plus autograft or BMA plus DBM.
autograft_standard: Calcaneal or iliac cancellous autograft at open bone grafting; most primary cases are percutaneous and use BMAC drawn from the iliac crest or calcaneus instead.
volume_note: No US annual count found. Forefoot fractures dominate foot-fracture incidence (123.9 per 100,000 per year in PMID 32499146) but the Jones subset is not broken out.
nonunion_note: Systematic review of 10 studies/998 patients comparing surgical and conservative treatment of zone-2 (Jones) fractures: nonunion 7/211 (3.3%) with surgical fixation vs 91/787 (11.6%) nonoperatively, total complications 8.5% vs 15.6% (Encinas 2026, JAAOS, PMID 42319275).
challenge: Nonunion is now sourced to a 2026 systematic review (surgical 3.3% vs conservative 11.6%). No US annual Jones-fracture count exists: the only nationwide fifth-metatarsal surgery epidemiology found is Japanese (PMID 40011147). Flag retained for volume.

name: Calcaneal fracture (intra-articular) with void fill after reduction

classifications.name: Sanders
classifications.summary: CT-based count of posterior-facet articular fragments on the coronal cut: I nondisplaced, II two-part, III three-part, IV four or more (comminuted); subtypes A-C by fracture-line position

classifications.name: Essex-Lopresti
classifications.summary: Plain-film pattern: tongue-type (fracture exits posteriorly through the tuberosity) versus joint-depression (posterior facet driven into the body)

why_biologic: Reduction of a depressed posterior facet leaves a cancellous void in the neutral triangle; a resorbable void filler or injectable calcium-phosphate cement is used to support the reduced facet and allow earlier weight-bearing. This is the clearest 'void fill' use in the foot. Cement augmentation has been studied in small series for 25 years; a Czech series found no outcome difference with or without filling, and a Dutch series associated void-filler use with wound complications through the extensile lateral approach.
autograft_standard: Historically iliac-crest or local cancellous autograft packed under the facet; many surgeons now leave the void empty or use a synthetic because the extensile approach already carries a high wound-complication rate and a second harvest site adds morbidity.
volume_note: No verified US count. Danish population data (PMID 32499146, 5,912 foot fractures) put all hindfoot fractures at 13.7 per 100,000 per year; the calcaneus is the most commonly fractured tarsal bone, and roughly three-quarters of calcaneal fractures are intra-articular in the older literature (that 75% figure is not verified in this sweep).
challenge: No US annual count found. Searched PubMed 2026-10-22 '(calcaneal fracture OR calcaneus fracture)[Title] AND (United States OR national OR nationwide) AND (incidence OR epidemiology OR trends)': no US national result; Danish population data (PMID 32499146) remain the only incidence source. The 75% intra-articular share is still unverified. Flag retained.

name: Subtalar, double and triple (hindfoot) arthrodesis
why_biologic: Posterior-facet preparation leaves a cancellous bed that surgeons fill with local autograft or a substitute; distraction or bone-block subtalar fusion after calcaneal malunion needs structural graft. Subtalar nonunion pooled at 6-10% (open 10.9%, arthroscopic 5.9%); revision subtalar fusion fails in about 20%; subtalar fusion after a prior tibiotalar fusion united in 80%. Augment's label covers hindfoot fusion, and the Augment pivotal cohort was largely subtalar, talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints.
autograft_standard: Local cancellous bone, calcaneal or proximal-tibial autograft, iliac-crest tricortical block for distraction arthrodesis; iliac harvest morbidity is the usual argument for substitutes.
volume_note: No subtalar-specific US count. All foot-and-ankle arthrodeses rose from 8.2 to 20.2 per 100,000 between 1994 and 2006 in NSAS/NHDS data, with outpatient volume up 415% (PMID 26213159); hindfoot joints are not broken out.
challenge: Searched PubMed 2026-10-22 (subtalar[Title] AND United States/national AND incidence/volume/utilization): no subtalar-specific national count. Flag retained.

name: Talar neck and body fracture; post-traumatic talar osteonecrosis

classifications.name: Hawkins (with Canale-Kelly modification)
classifications.summary: Talar neck: I nondisplaced; II displaced with subtalar subluxation or dislocation (IIA subluxed, IIB dislocated); III displaced with subtalar and tibiotalar dislocation; IV adds talonavicular dislocation. Osteonecrosis risk rises with grade.

why_biologic: Acute fixation uses no biologic. The biologic use case is the downstream salvage: talar osteonecrosis or collapse leading to tibiotalocalcaneal or pantalar arthrodesis with a structural bone block (femoral-head allograft), bulk autograft, or a custom 3D-printed titanium cage, often with BMAC or rhBMP-2 used off-label by the surgeon. Core decompression with BMAC for early AVN is reported only in small series.
autograft_standard: For salvage fusion the standard is iliac-crest structural autograft or fibular strut; volume is limited for the large defects seen after talar collapse, which is why bulk allograft and metal cages dominate.
volume_note: Rare injury; no US volume source found. Talus fractures are a small fraction of hindfoot fractures (hindfoot incidence 13.7 per 100,000 per year in PMID 32499146).
challenge: No US volume source. Searched PubMed 2026-10-22 (talus[Title] AND United States/national AND incidence/epidemiology): only a Finnish register study (PMID 39702100) and a US-military osteochondral-lesion study (PMID 22224323) were returned; neither gives a US talus-fracture count. Flag retained.

name: Tibiotalocalcaneal (TTC) and tibiocalcaneal arthrodesis, including bulk-defect salvage
why_biologic: The highest-nonunion fusion in the foot and ankle: 27.1% pooled in an umbrella meta-analysis, with much of the indication mix being failed total ankle replacement, talar osteonecrosis, Charcot, and infection. Large defects are filled with femoral-head structural allograft (union 67.4% pooled; 50% in a 32-patient series where every diabetic failed) or a 3D-printed titanium cage (union 88-89% pooled), and surgeons layer BMAC, DBM, and off-label rhBMP-2 onto the construct. Revision TTC with a retrograde nail achieved a stable limb in about 70% with or without BMP-2 in a 23-patient series.
autograft_standard: Fibular strut (resected distal fibula) or iliac-crest autograft; volume is insufficient for the multi-centimeter defects that define the salvage subgroup, which is why structural allograft and cages dominate.
volume_note: No US annual count found; a niche, high-acuity procedure concentrated in tertiary foot-and-ankle and limb-salvage centers.
challenge: No US annual count. Searched PubMed 2026-10-22 (tibiotalocalcaneal/ankle arthrodesis AND United States/national): NIS ankle-arthrodesis counts (PMID 39931642) do not separate TTC from tibiotalar fusion. Union for 3D-titanium TTC in critical defects pooled 88.2% in 15 studies/142 patients (PMID 41724588). Flag retained.

name: Charcot neuroarthropathy midfoot and hindfoot reconstruction

classifications.name: Eichenholtz
classifications.summary: Stage 0 prodromal (warm, swollen, normal films); I development/fragmentation; II coalescence; III consolidation/remodeling

classifications.name: Brodsky anatomic
classifications.summary: Type 1 midfoot (tarsometatarsal and naviculocuneiform, about 60%); 2 hindfoot (subtalar, talonavicular, calcaneocuboid); 3A ankle; 3B calcaneal tuberosity

why_biologic: Neuropathic, osteopenic, often ulcerated and infected bone with very high nonunion and hardware-failure rates; surgeons use extended internal fixation (beams, bolts, plates) or external fixation and routinely add BMAC, DBM, PRP, structural allograft, and off-label rhBMP-2 because autograft volume is inadequate and the host is compromised. A systematic review of intramedullary beaming found high nonunion and complication rates with poor-quality evidence; external fixation was 8 times more likely to show radiographic nonunion than internal fixation in a 2016 review. Infected Charcot is where antibiotic-eluting carriers enter.
autograft_standard: Iliac-crest or proximal-tibial autograft; the volume needed after wedge resection usually exceeds what can be harvested, and diabetic hosts tolerate a second site poorly.
volume_note: No US procedure count found. Texas hospital-discharge data show rising age-standardized Charcot rates in diabetic patients from 2006 to 2016 with increasing amputations (PMID 38944563). Charcot midfoot-fusion TTC nails pooled a 3.3% nonunion rate in a 2025 meta-analysis of 147 patients, a figure most foot-and-ankle surgeons would treat as optimistic.
challenge: Any single Charcot nonunion percentage will be challenged because series count stable fibrous nonunion with a plantigrade, ulcer-free foot as success (PMID 34587806, PMID 25862129); the 11.9% pooled figure (PMID 38548584) is the best-sourced number, and the 3.3% TTC-nail figure is optimistic.
nonunion_note: Proportional meta-analysis of 30 studies/492 internal-fixation Charcot reconstructions: nonunion 11.9% (95% CI 6.6-18.1), deep infection 6.7%, amputation after infection 36.6% (Tsikopoulos 2024, PMID 38548584). Union definitions differ: Kavarthapu 2021 counted 9/15 midfoot fusions (60%) with the other six as 'stable and painless fibrous nonunion' and all limbs salvaged (PMID 34587806); Mittlmeier 2015 states the outcome 'does not depend on definite osseous healing of the arthrodesis' (PMID 25862129).

name: Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) fracture-dislocation: ORIF versus primary arthrodesis

classifications.name: Myerson (modified Hardcastle)
classifications.summary: A total incongruity of the tarsometatarsal joint; B partial incongruity (B1 medial column, B2 lateral columns); C divergent (C1 partial, C2 total)

classifications.name: Nunley-Vertullo
classifications.summary: Subtle (ligamentous, athletic) injuries: stage I no diastasis on weight-bearing films, II 2-5 mm diastasis without arch collapse, III diastasis with loss of arch height

why_biologic: Primary arthrodesis of the medial two or three tarsometatarsal joints has become common for purely ligamentous injuries because it halves reoperation versus ORIF in randomized data; the fusion bed is small and surgeons pack it with local autograft, DBM, or a cellular allograft. In ORIF there is no biologic role. Nonunion after primary arthrodesis is uncommon but not pooled in the studies found.
autograft_standard: Local bone from joint preparation or calcaneal/proximal-tibial cancellous autograft; small volumes needed, so donor-site morbidity is modest.
volume_note: US TriNetX Collaborative Network 2014-2024: 21,964 primary Lisfranc injuries presenting to EDs or ambulatory settings, overall incidence 22.4 per 100,000 person-years, peaking at 33.6 per 100,000 at ages 40-44 (PMID 40839129). Lisfranc injuries are about 0.2% of all fractures (PMID 26022112); midfoot fracture incidence is 6.5 per 100,000 per year in Danish data (PMID 32499146). No US operative count.
challenge: TriNetX incidence is a network-based estimate (participating health systems), not a census; surgical-intervention rates are in the paper, not extracted here.

name: Distal femur fracture (supracondylar / intercondylar, including periprosthetic above a TKA)

classifications.name: AO/OTA 33
classifications.summary: Distal femur: 33-A extra-articular (A1 simple, A2 metaphyseal wedge, A3 metaphyseal complex), 33-B partial articular (B1 lateral sagittal, B2 medial sagittal, B3 coronal/Hoffa), 33-C complete articular (C1 simple articular and metaphyseal, C2 simple articular with multifragmentary metaphysis, C3 multifragmentary articular).

classifications.name: Periprosthetic (Lewis-Rorabeck / Su)
classifications.summary: Rorabeck I undisplaced with stable prosthesis, II displaced with stable prosthesis, III loose or failing prosthesis; Su types by fracture level relative to the femoral component.

why_biologic: This is the one distal-femur situation where a bone void filler is routinely considered: metaphyseal comminution or impaction in osteoporotic bone leaves a void behind a lateral locking plate or retrograde nail, and surgeons fill it with calcium phosphate cement, calcium sulfate/hydroxyapatite composites, allograft chips or DBM to resist collapse and support the construct. Evidence is biomechanical and retrospective (for example a cadaver study of CPC-augmented condylar screws, Bäumlein 2020). No RCT shows that any filler improves union or reoperation in distal femur fractures; void fillers are labeled as 'not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure' which is at odds with how they are used here. Medial comminution with bone loss in young patients is a nonunion risk where autograft at index or revision is used.
autograft_standard: Autogenous cancellous graft (iliac crest or RIA) for medial defects or at nonunion revision; morbidity and added OR time are the trade-off.
volume_note: No authoritative US annual count found; distal femur fractures are roughly 4-7% of femoral fractures in secondary sources and periprosthetic distal femur fractures are rising with TKA volume.
challenge: No US annual count found. Searched PubMed 2026-10-22 '(distal femur OR distal femoral)[Title] AND (United States OR nationwide OR national) AND (incidence OR epidemiology OR trends)': only a Danish nationwide cohort of 60,823 knee fractures (PMID 31795876) was returned. Flag retained; the 4-7% share of femoral fractures remains a secondary-source figure.

name: Femoral shaft fracture

classifications.name: AO/OTA 32
classifications.summary: Femoral diaphysis: 32-A simple (spiral, oblique, transverse), 32-B wedge (intact or fragmentary), 32-C multifragmentary (segmental or complex).

classifications.name: Winquist-Hansen
classifications.summary: Comminution grades 0-IV by the amount of cortical contact remaining; historically used to decide on nail locking.

classifications.name: Gustilo-Anderson (if open)
classifications.summary: Open-fracture grades I-IIIC by wound size, contamination, periosteal stripping and vascular injury.

why_biologic: None for the closed fracture: reamed, statically locked intramedullary nailing unites well over 90% of femoral shaft fractures without any graft, and reaming itself deposits autologous marrow at the fracture. Biologics are relevant only for open fractures with bone loss (segmental defects, see femoral-segmental-defect) and for nonunion. Infuse (rhBMP-2) is labeled only for acute open TIBIAL shaft fractures with IM nailing within 14 days; any femoral use is off-label.
autograft_standard: Not used in primary nailing. For defects and nonunions the benchmark is autograft (iliac crest, or RIA harvest from the contralateral or ipsilateral femoral canal).
volume_note: No single authoritative US annual count found in public sources; femoral shaft fractures are far less common than hip fractures and skew to high-energy trauma in younger adults.
challenge: No US annual count found. Searched PubMed 2026-10-22 (femoral shaft[Title] AND United States/nationwide/national AND incidence/epidemiology/trends): only Swedish national data (6,409 inpatients 1998-2004, 10 per 100,000 person-years, PMID 19171340) and pediatric US practice-pattern papers. Flag retained.

name: Femoral shaft nonunion (aseptic, after nailing or plating)

classifications.name: Weber-Cech
classifications.summary: Hypertrophic (biologically active, mechanically unstable) versus atrophic/oligotrophic (biologically inert) nonunion; dictates whether a biologic is needed at all.

classifications.name: Non-Union Scoring System (NUSS)
classifications.summary: Points for bone quality, prior surgeries, infection, soft tissue and host factors; higher scores push toward biologic augmentation or specialist referral.

why_biologic: Hypertrophic nonunions are fixed with exchange nailing (reaming re-seeds the site with marrow) and need no graft. Atrophic nonunions and those with bone loss get open debridement, compression plating or nail-plate constructs, and a biologic: iliac crest or RIA autograft first, with DBM or a ceramic as an extender, BMAC (Hernigou's percutaneous technique, validated in tibial nonunion with union in 53 of 60, PMID 15995108), and historically rhBMP-7 (OP-1, HDE-approved for recalcitrant long-bone nonunion, no longer available in the US). rhBMP-2 (Infuse) is used off-label by some surgeons; its label covers only acute open tibial fractures.
autograft_standard: Iliac crest bone graft is the historical gold standard; RIA autograft from the femoral canal matched its union rate (82% versus 86%) with less donor-site pain in a 133-patient RCT (Dawson 2014, Synthes-supported RIA kits).
volume_note: Femoral shaft nonunion after reamed nailing is usually quoted below 5-10% (secondary sources); no US annual count.
challenge: Nonunion after reamed nailing remains a secondary-source range (<5-10%); no US count. Searched PubMed 2026-10-22 for femoral shaft nonunion incidence in US databases: none found. Flag retained.

name: Critical-size femoral bone defect (open fracture with bone loss, infected nonunion, tumor resection)

classifications.name: Defect size
classifications.summary: Defects longer than roughly 2-3 cm or more than 50% of cortical circumference are unlikely to bridge without reconstruction; above 5-6 cm distraction osteogenesis or vascularized bone is usually considered.

classifications.name: Gustilo-Anderson IIIB/IIIC
classifications.summary: Open fractures with periosteal stripping or vascular injury where bone loss is common.

why_biologic: This is the highest-biologic-intensity trauma scenario in the femur. The Masquelet induced-membrane technique stages a PMMA spacer (sometimes antibiotic-loaded), then fills the membrane-lined cavity with autograft, typically RIA-harvested, with DBM, allograft chips or a ceramic as a volume extender and, in some centers, rhBMP or BMAC; pooled union is roughly 85-90% with reinterventions common (Morelli 2016 meta-analysis of 17 papers, 427 patients). Antibiotic-eluting fillers (Cerament G, Stimulan with surgeon-added antibiotic) are used in the infected subset, and Cerament G's 2024 510(k) now covers open fractures in the extremities.
autograft_standard: RIA autograft is the practical benchmark for large volumes (mean 37.7 cc in Dawson 2014), supplemented by iliac crest when more is needed; donor-site morbidity, finite supply and a second surgical site are the downsides.
volume_note: No public US count; these are rare, concentrated in Level 1 trauma centers.

name: Periprosthetic femoral fracture around a hip arthroplasty stem

classifications.name: Vancouver (Duncan-Masri)
classifications.summary: A trochanteric (AG greater, AL lesser); B around or just below the stem: B1 stem well fixed, B2 stem loose with good bone stock, B3 stem loose with poor bone stock; C well below the stem. Unified Classification System extends the same logic to all joints.

why_biologic: B1 and C fractures are plated; B2/B3 get a revision stem. The classic biologic here is the cortical onlay strut allograft used as a 'biological plate' with cerclage, alone or with a plate: 39 of 40 fractures united in the multicenter series by Haddad and Duncan (2002). Modern locking plates (91% union in a pooled review) have reduced strut use, and one series reported 18 of 19 B1 fractures healing with plates and no struts. For B3 bone loss, impaction allograft or allograft-prosthesis composites are revision-arthroplasty territory.
autograft_standard: Autograft is rarely used; the structural need is met by allograft struts, which carry disease-transmission (low) and stress-shielding/resorption concerns.
volume_note: Periprosthetic femoral fractures occur after roughly 0.1-6% of THAs (Graham 2013 review); absolute US counts rise with the installed base of arthroplasties.

name: Atypical femoral fracture (bisphosphonate- or denosumab-associated)

classifications.name: ASBMR Task Force 2013 case definition
classifications.summary: Major features: fracture distal to the lesser trochanter and proximal to the supracondylar flare, minimal or no trauma, transverse or short-oblique origin at the lateral cortex, complete or incomplete (lateral cortex only), non- or minimally comminuted, periosteal or endosteal thickening ('beaking') at the fracture site. Minor features include generalized cortical thickening, prodromal thigh pain and bilaterality.

classifications.name: Complete versus incomplete
classifications.summary: Complete fractures are nailed; incomplete fractures with pain are usually prophylactically nailed, without pain may be observed with drug holiday.

why_biologic: Treatment is cephalomedullary nailing plus stopping the antiresorptive; the biologic question is whether an anabolic (teriparatide, abaloparatide, romosozumab) speeds a fracture that heals slowly because remodeling is suppressed. The ASBMR task force called the teriparatide evidence 'inconsistent'; the best prospective data (Watts 2017, open-label, n=14, Lilly-supported) found no consistent healing effect and said teriparatide 'should not be relied on to aid in healing'. Everything else is case reports. All anabolic use for healing is off-label.
autograft_standard: Not used at index; delayed union or nonunion is treated by exchange nailing with or without autograft.
volume_note: Absolute risk on bisphosphonates is low, 3.2-50 per 100,000 person-years, rising toward roughly 100 per 100,000 with long-term use (ASBMR 2013); no US annual count.

name: Scaphoid fracture and nonunion

classifications.name: Herbert (in words)
classifications.summary: Type A stable acute (A1 tubercle, A2 incomplete waist), Type B unstable acute (B1 distal oblique, B2 complete waist, B3 proximal pole, B4 trans-scaphoid perilunate), Type C delayed union, Type D established nonunion (D1 fibrous, D2 pseudarthrosis).

classifications.name: Mayo / Russe (in words)
classifications.summary: Location-based: distal third, waist, proximal pole; and fracture-line orientation (horizontal oblique, transverse, vertical oblique).

why_biologic: The nonunion site is debrided and grafted because the proximal pole has a retrograde blood supply and sclerotic ends; graft restores length (humpback correction) and supplies osteogenic bone. Vascularized grafts (1,2-ICSRA distal radius, medial femoral condyle free flap) are used for avascular proximal poles. Off-the-shelf biologics (DBM, BMAC, rhBMP-7 historically) have only small series or a 17-patient RCT behind them.
autograft_standard: Nonvascularized iliac crest (Matti-Russe or Fisk-Fernandez wedge) or distal radius cancellous/corticocancellous graft with a headless compression screw. Union 79-96% for ICBG and 87-100% for distal radius graft with no significant difference, but ICBG carries 20% donor-site pain or hematoma vs 0% (Ghaderi 2026 meta, n=166, PMID:42537801). Vascularized vs nonvascularized: pooled OR 1.57 for union, not significant, with shorter time to union for vascularized graft (Guria 2025 meta of 5 RCTs, PMID:39974267).
volume_note: Scaphoid fractures are the most common carpal fracture (70%) and the second most common wrist fracture. Adjusted true incidence 22 per 100,000 person-years in Sweden (Sward 2019, PMID:31106681); around 14% progressed to nonunion in a 16,691-fracture Swiss insurance cohort (Rothenfluh 2025, PMID:41258412). US-specific incidence not found.

name: Distal radius corrective osteotomy (opening-wedge void)

classifications.name: Not classified by fracture scheme
classifications.summary: Dorsal or volar opening-wedge osteotomy for symptomatic malunion; the gap was traditionally filled with iliac crest tricortical autograft.

why_biologic: This is the one wrist indication where a void filler had a defensible role, because the osteotomy gap is surgeon-created. Two double-blind RCTs now show that with a volar plate and maintained cortical contact, filling the gap with HydroSet calcium phosphate cement (Andreasson 2020, PMID:32472263) or an injectable bone substitute (Angelomenos 2025, n=42, PMID:40063246) does not change function or micromotion vs leaving the gap empty.
autograft_standard: Tricortical iliac crest wedge; prolongs surgery and adds donor-site morbidity, and is increasingly omitted.
volume_note: Small elective volume; no US figure found.

name: Distal radius fracture (void fill in osteoporotic bone)

classifications.name: AO/OTA 23 (now 2R3)
classifications.summary: A extra-articular, B partial articular, C complete articular; metaphyseal comminution subtypes drive void size.

classifications.name: Frykman (in words)
classifications.summary: Types I-VIII by radiocarpal and radioulnar joint involvement and presence of an ulnar styloid fracture.

classifications.name: Fernandez (in words)
classifications.summary: Mechanism-based: I bending (Colles/Smith), II shearing (Barton), III compression (die-punch), IV avulsion/fracture-dislocation, V high-energy combined.

why_biologic: Historically a calcium phosphate cement (Norian SRS) was injected to hold the reduction of an osteoporotic metaphyseal void after closed reduction or pinning. Volar locking plates made the void mechanically irrelevant: the only RCT of cement plus volar plate (Kim 2011, n=50 fractures, PMID:21471414) found no benefit, beta-TCP granules added nothing to plating (Jakubietz 2011, PMID:21600042), and injectable DBM added nothing to K-wire fixation (D'Agostino 2013, PMID:24151272). Today biologic use in distal radius fractures is rare and hard to justify on evidence.
autograft_standard: Autogenous cancellous graft was the historical comparator in the Cochrane review (Handoll 2008, 10 trials, 874 adults, PMID:18425972); it did not change outcomes with external fixation and carried one serious donor-site complication.
volume_note: Distal radius and ulna fractures are the most common US upper-extremity fracture at 16.2 per 10,000 persons per year (Karl 2015, PMID:25714441; extrapolated ~500,000/yr), with bimodal pediatric and elderly peaks (Nellans 2012, PMID:22554654). Nonunion is rare; there were no nonunions in either arm of Kim 2011.

name: Metacarpal and phalangeal fractures

classifications.name: Descriptive (in words)
classifications.summary: By bone (metacarpal, proximal/middle/distal phalanx), location (head, neck, shaft, base), pattern (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted) and named injuries (boxer's, Bennett, Rolando, mallet).

why_biologic: Rarely biologic. These fractures unite reliably with splinting, K-wires, intramedullary screws or plates; nonunion is uncommon and when it occurs is treated with debridement, local or distal radius cancellous autograft and rigid fixation (Czerniecki 2024, PMID:37979984). Cancellous allograft chips or DBM are occasionally used for comminuted defects. This is the highest-volume, lowest-biologic segment in the upper extremity.
autograft_standard: Distal radius or iliac crest cancellous autograft for nonunion or bone loss; rarely needed.
volume_note: Phalangeal (12.5 per 10,000) and metacarpal (8.4 per 10,000) fractures are the second and third most common US upper-extremity fractures (Karl 2015, PMID:25714441; extrapolated ~386,000 and ~259,000/yr). A claims database identified 80,787 metacarpal fixations over 2010-2022 (Kishan 2025, PMID:40583362). Nonunion rate not quantified in the sources found (unverified).

name: Radial head fracture

classifications.name: Mason / Hotchkiss-modified (in words)
classifications.summary: Type I minimally displaced, Type II displaced partial articular (>2 mm) amenable to fixation, Type III comminuted whole-head, Type IV with elbow dislocation.

why_biologic: None in practice. Fixation of fragmented heads is prone to failure and nonunion, and the answer is radial head arthroplasty, not a graft (Duckworth 2013, PMID:23365021). Listed to close the loop on elbow trauma.
autograft_standard: Not applicable.
volume_note: No reliable US volume source found; radial head fractures are commonly cited as the most frequent elbow fracture in adults (unverified).
challenge: No US volume source found. Searched PubMed 2026-10-22 '(radial head[Title]) AND (United States OR national OR nationwide) AND (incidence OR epidemiology OR trends)': the only hit is pediatric radial head subluxation in NEISS (PMID 34363491), not adult fractures. 'Most frequent adult elbow fracture' remains unverified. Flag retained.

name: Olecranon fracture and olecranon osteotomy

classifications.name: Mayo (in words)
classifications.summary: Type I undisplaced, Type II displaced-stable, Type III displaced-unstable; A noncomminuted, B comminuted.

classifications.name: AO/OTA 2U1
classifications.summary: Proximal ulna segment; A extra-articular, B partial articular, C complete articular (2018 revision).

why_biologic: Almost never. Tension band, plate or suture fixation without graft; the olecranon's cancellous bed heals reliably. Delayed union after olecranon osteotomy (used to approach distal humerus fractures) was 4.2% pooled (Feinstein 2023, PMID:37790831). Included to document a no-biologic segment the same reps call on.
autograft_standard: Not applicable; comminuted defects occasionally receive local cancellous graft.
volume_note: Olecranon fractures are ~1% of upper-extremity fractures (Matar 2014 Cochrane, PMID:25426876). No US biologic volume.

name: Both-bone forearm fracture and forearm nonunion

classifications.name: AO/OTA 2R2 / 2U2
classifications.summary: Radial and ulnar diaphysis; A simple, B wedge, C multifragmentary. Monteggia (ulna fracture with radial head dislocation, Bado I-IV) and Galeazzi variants named separately.

why_biologic: Acute both-bone fractures are plated without graft; even 1970s compression plating gave 97.9% (radius) and 96.3% (ulna) union with iliac graft used only in 26% severely comminuted cases (Anderson 1975, PMID:1091653). Biologics enter for atrophic nonunion, segmental defects and Monteggia ulna nonunion, where cancellous autograft, structural allograft or vascularized fibula are used.
autograft_standard: Iliac crest cancellous autograft with compression plating for atrophic nonunion; free vascularized fibula for large defects (case-level evidence only).
volume_note: No US volume found for adult forearm nonunion. Ulna nonunion was the leading reason for revision (28%) after Monteggia injuries in a pooled review of 651 cases (Weber 2023, PMID:36056930).

name: Chronic long-bone osteomyelitis: single-stage debridement with antibiotic-eluting dead-space filler

classifications.name: Cierny-Mader
classifications.summary: Anatomic type I-IV and host class A-C; single-stage antibiotic-biocomposite series were mostly type III-IV, class B hosts, and most defects were in the tibia.

why_biologic: Dead-space management is the step that determines recurrence; a resorbable carrier that elutes gentamicin, vancomycin or tobramycin fills the cavity, sterilizes it locally and is replaced by bone, removing the second operation needed to retrieve PMMA beads. This is the only trauma-adjacent application where an FDA-authorized antibiotic-device combination exists (CERAMENT G, De Novo 2022) and where CMS has created product-specific inpatient payment (NTAP FY2026, DRG reassignment FY2027).
autograft_standard: Debridement plus PMMA antibiotic beads and staged autograft; or antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate beads mixed off-label in the US. Pooled eradication with antibiotic calcium sulfate 92% (917 patients, no RCTs) and 96% with gentamicin CS/HA in a 100-patient prospective series.
volume_note: Inpatient osteomyelitis is paid under MS-DRGs 539-541; counts not retrieved. Bonesupport reports CERAMENT G US sales of USD 18.3 million in Q2 2025 (+84%), the best public proxy for adoption.

name: General long-bone nonunion (femur, tibia, humerus, forearm): biologic augmentation under the diamond concept

classifications.name: Diamond concept (Giannoudis 2007)
classifications.summary: Successful healing needs osteogenic cells, osteoinductive growth factor, osteoconductive scaffold and mechanical stability, plus host optimization (vascularity, infection control, metabolic work-up). Hypertrophic nonunions need stability; atrophic need biology.

why_biologic: Reference application for other regions: a biologic is chosen by which diamond element is missing. BMAC or marrow injection adds cells, rhBMP (OP-1 historically, rhBMP-2 off-label) adds growth factor, DBM/ceramic/allograft add scaffold; PRP evidence is weak and cellular allografts have no trauma evidence.
autograft_standard: Autogenous cancellous graft (ICBG or RIA) with revision fixation remains the comparator in every RCT; donor-site complications 19.4% for ICBG. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 15 RCTs (1,286 patients) ranked PRP+autograft and PRP+BMAC highest for healing time, but the trials are small and heterogeneous.
volume_note: US claims data: 4.9% of 309,330 fractures progressed to nonunion within 12 months (2011 cohort); 5-10% is the commonly cited range. No annual nonunion procedure count found.

name: Femoral head osteonecrosis (AVN), core decompression with biologic augmentation

classifications.name: ARCO (2019 revision)
classifications.summary: Stage I MRI-only, II radiographic changes without collapse, IIIA subchondral fracture or collapse under 2 mm, IIIB collapse 2 mm or more, IV osteoarthritis. Biologic augmentation is a pre-collapse (I-II) procedure.

classifications.name: Ficat-Arlet / Steinberg
classifications.summary: Older staging by radiographic change, crescent sign, collapse and joint-space loss; Steinberg adds lesion size.

why_biologic: Core decompression alone has mediocre results; adding a biologic to the decompression track is where most hip 'orthobiologic' activity sits. Options: autologous bone marrow concentrate injected into the track (Hernigou's technique; 125-patient bilateral-hip RCT with 25-year follow-up, 24% versus 76% conversion to THA, PMID 29744647; meta-analysis OR 0.2 for collapse, PMID 26220203), backfill with a calcium sulfate/calcium phosphate composite (Pro-Dense core decompression kit, K072597; Civinini 2012 series) or a ceramic such as Cerament, non-vascularized or vascularized fibular graft, and, as negative evidence, cultured osteoblastic cells (Preob, phase 3 negative, PMID 36961220) and BMAC in post-collapse stage III (negative double-blind RCT, PMID 28988340). Most positive data come from a single French center.
autograft_standard: Free vascularized fibular graft (Urbaniak) is the structural autograft benchmark for larger pre-collapse lesions; long operation and donor-site morbidity restrict it to specialized centers.
volume_note: A 2010-2020 nationwide US claims study identified 64,739 patients with osteonecrosis of the femoral head who underwent hip surgery, about 5,900 surgical cases per year, and cites an estimated incidence of more than 20,000 new ONFH patients annually in the US (PMID 37001624). The 20,000 figure is an estimate quoted by that paper, not a measured count; the proportion treated with core decompression vs arthroplasty is in the paper's tables.
challenge: The surgical count comes from a commercial claims database (not all-payer) and the '>20,000 per year' incidence is a literature estimate the paper repeats; both should be presented as such.

name: Acetabular and pelvic ring fractures

classifications.name: Letournel-Judet (acetabulum)
classifications.summary: Five elementary patterns (posterior wall, posterior column, anterior wall, anterior column, transverse) and five associated patterns (posterior column plus posterior wall, transverse plus posterior wall, T-shaped, anterior column plus posterior hemitransverse, both-column).

classifications.name: Tile (pelvic ring)
classifications.summary: A stable (ring intact), B rotationally unstable but vertically stable (open-book or lateral compression), C rotationally and vertically unstable.

classifications.name: Young-Burgess (pelvic ring)
classifications.summary: By force vector: lateral compression I-III, anteroposterior compression I-III, vertical shear, combined mechanism.

classifications.name: Fragility fractures of the pelvis (Rommens)
classifications.summary: FFP I-IV by anterior and posterior ring involvement and displacement in osteoporotic patients.

why_biologic: Essentially none. Acetabular and pelvic ring fractures are fixed with plates, screws and percutaneous sacroiliac screws; the pelvis is richly vascularized and nonunion is rare. The only biologic-adjacent uses are (a) bone void fillers packed behind marginal-impaction or posterior-wall defects of the acetabulum (case series only), (b) cement augmentation of sacroiliac screws or sacroplasty in fragility fractures (PMMA; handled by the spine/VCF agent), and (c) off-label teriparatide to speed healing of osteoporotic pelvic fractures, which rests on one small open-label RCT (Peichl 2011, n=65, not retrieved here) and is under re-study (NCT06303284, Calgary, not yet recruiting).
autograft_standard: Not applicable to primary fixation. Acetabular bone loss at later arthroplasty uses structural or morselized allograft, which belongs to arthroplasty rather than trauma.
volume_note: NIS 2000-2009: 24,059 inpatients with unstable pelvic fracture, about 2,400 per year, in-hospital mortality 8.3% (PMID 24398776). NIS 2011-2018: 123,936 nonoperatively managed low-energy pelvic fractures, about 15,500 per year, mean age 68.7, 70% female (PMID 37564706). NIS 2016-2022: 20,169 weighted internal fixations of pelvic ring fractures, about 2,900 per year (PMID 42690542). Pelvic fractures are about 3% of all fractures in secondary sources.
challenge: The three NIS figures use different case definitions (unstable fracture, low-energy nonoperative, operatively fixed ring) and cannot be summed; acetabular ORIF volume is not separately counted here.

name: Femoral neck fracture (intracapsular hip fracture)

classifications.name: Garden I-IV
classifications.summary: I incomplete/valgus-impacted; II complete, undisplaced; III complete, partially displaced; IV complete, fully displaced. Clinically collapsed to undisplaced (I-II) versus displaced (III-IV).

classifications.name: Pauwels I-III
classifications.summary: Fracture-line angle from horizontal: I under 30 degrees, II 30-50 degrees, III over 50 degrees (vertical, high shear, highest nonunion and osteonecrosis risk).

classifications.name: AO/OTA 31-B
classifications.summary: Femoral neck: B1 subcapital with slight displacement, B2 transcervical, B3 subcapital displaced (2007 scheme; the 2018 revision regroups by displacement).

why_biologic: Almost none. Displaced fractures in older patients get hemi- or total hip arthroplasty; undisplaced and young-patient fractures get cannulated screws, a sliding hip screw, or the Femoral Neck System. No biologic is routinely implanted. Biologics enter only (a) as off-label pharmacologic adjuncts (teriparatide tested in an industry RCT with no healing benefit; romosozumab likewise), (b) in salvage of nonunion or osteonecrosis (see femoral-neck-nonunion and femoral-head-osteonecrosis records), and (c) historically, calcium phosphate cement augmentation of screws (Norian SRS, studied in small Scandinavian trials in the 2000s and not adopted).
autograft_standard: Not applicable to primary fixation. For salvage in young patients the benchmark is valgus intertrochanteric osteotomy (Pauwels/Marti) with or without free vascularized fibular autograft; donor-site morbidity and a long operation limit the latter.
volume_note: CDC analysis of 2019 HCUP and NVSS data: 318,797 ED visits, 290,130 hospitalizations and 7,731 deaths for hip fracture among US adults 65+, with falls causing about 88% of hospitalizations (Moreland 2022, PMID 36210739). This is the primary source behind the commonly quoted 'roughly 300,000 per year'. Medicare claims show age-adjusted rates in women 65+ fell 2002-2012 then plateaued 2013-2015 (Lewiecki 2018, PMID 29282482). Neck vs trochanteric split is not reported in these sources.
challenge: The 290,130 count is hospitalizations in adults 65+ (all hip fracture types), not femoral-neck fractures specifically and not under-65 patients.

name: Femoral neck nonunion (and neglected femoral neck fracture)

classifications.name: Pauwels (applied to nonunion)
classifications.summary: Vertical (Pauwels III) fracture lines are the main predictor of nonunion after fixation; valgus osteotomy converts shear to compression.

classifications.name: Viability of the femoral head
classifications.summary: Nonunion with a viable head is salvageable (osteotomy or grafting); nonunion with osteonecrosis or collapse usually means arthroplasty.

why_biologic: In older patients the answer is arthroplasty, no biologic. In young patients with a viable head the biology is supplied mechanically (valgus intertrochanteric osteotomy) or by a vascularized or non-vascularized fibular graft placed across the neck (free vascularized fibula series report union in all 13 and 29 patients in two small series). Percutaneous BMAC injection is reported by Hernigou for long-bone nonunions generally but not specifically validated for the femoral neck. No commercial bone graft substitute has evidence here.
autograft_standard: Free vascularized fibular autograft or non-vascularized fibular strut (autograft or allograft) plus revision fixation; the vascularized graft carries donor-site morbidity and microsurgical complexity.
volume_note: Nonunion follows roughly 10-30% of displaced femoral neck fractures treated with fixation in young adults (secondary sources); no US annual count.
challenge: Nonunion after fixation of displaced femoral neck fractures in young adults (10-30%) remains a secondary-source range; no US annual count was found (searched PubMed 2026-10-22 for femoral neck nonunion incidence in US databases). Flag retained.

name: Intertrochanteric / pertrochanteric fracture (extracapsular hip fracture)

classifications.name: AO/OTA 31-A
classifications.summary: Trochanteric region: A1 simple two-part pertrochanteric (stable), A2 multifragmentary pertrochanteric with lesser-trochanter/posteromedial comminution (unstable), A3 intertrochanteric including reverse-oblique and transverse patterns (unstable, lateral wall involved).

classifications.name: Evans / Jensen
classifications.summary: Stable versus unstable by integrity of the posteromedial cortex and reducibility; largely superseded by AO/OTA 31-A in US trauma practice.

why_biologic: Standard care is a cephalomedullary nail (or sliding hip screw for stable A1 patterns) with no biologic. The one place a 'biologic-adjacent' material enters routinely is augmentation of the lag screw or helical blade in osteoporotic bone: PMMA (Traumacem V+, cleared 2017 specifically for the TFN-Advanced nail) and, historically, resorbable calcium phosphate cement (Norian SRS, Mattsson RCTs 2004-2005). The PFNA augmentation RCT (Kammerlander 2018, n=223) showed no difference in the primary mobility endpoint and a trend toward fewer implant-related revisions. Pharmacologic adjuncts after fixation (zoledronate for secondary fracture prevention; teriparatide versus risedronate in a Lilly-funded RCT) are about the next fracture and function, not union of this one.
autograft_standard: Not applicable; these fractures unite reliably with hardware alone. Failure mode is mechanical (cut-out, varus collapse), not biological.
volume_note: US hip-fracture hospitalizations in adults 65+ numbered 290,130 in 2019 (CDC analysis of HCUP, PMID 36210739). Trochanteric fractures are usually described as roughly half of hip fractures in secondary sources; no primary US source splitting neck from trochanteric fractures was found.
challenge: The total is primary (CDC/HCUP 2019); the 'roughly half' trochanteric share is still a secondary-source proportion.

name: Subtrochanteric femur fracture

classifications.name: AO/OTA 32 (subtrochanteric qualifier)
classifications.summary: In the 2018 AO/OTA revision subtrochanteric fractures are coded as femoral diaphyseal (32) with a proximal-third/subtrochanteric qualifier; older practice grouped reverse-oblique patterns under 31-A3. Russell-Taylor (I/II by piriformis-fossa and lesser-trochanter involvement) is still used in words to pick a nail entry point.

why_biologic: None in primary treatment. Cephalomedullary nailing with careful reduction is the standard; delayed union is usually attributed to varus malreduction or an atypical (bisphosphonate-related) fracture rather than a biological deficit. Biologics (autograft, BMAC, off-label teriparatide) are considered only at nonunion revision. See atypical-femoral-fracture for the bisphosphonate-related subset.
autograft_standard: At nonunion revision: exchange nailing with or without autograft (iliac crest or RIA-harvested femoral canal autograft).
volume_note: No reliable public US count separate from hip fractures; subtrochanteric fractures are usually quoted as 10-30% of proximal femur fractures in secondary sources.
challenge: No US count separate from hip fractures. Searched PubMed 2026-10-22 (subtrochanteric[Title] AND United States/nationwide/national AND incidence/trends): only a Korean claims study (PMID 22618268). The 10-30% share remains secondary. Flag retained.

subregion: any upper-extremity long bone or hand
name: Upper-extremity osteomyelitis and fracture-related infection (dead-space management)

classifications.name: Cierny-Mader (in words)
classifications.summary: Anatomic type I medullary, II superficial, III localized, IV diffuse; host class A normal, B compromised (local/systemic), C treatment worse than disease.

classifications.name: Fracture-related infection consensus (in words)
classifications.summary: Confirmatory criteria (fistula, purulence, two positive cultures, histology) vs suggestive criteria; early, delayed and late by time from fixation.

why_biologic: After debridement the dead space is filled with an absorbable carrier that elutes antibiotic locally and is replaced by bone, avoiding a second surgery to remove PMMA beads. Antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate (Stimulan, mixed by the surgeon, off-label in the US) and the gentamicin-eluting calcium sulfate/hydroxyapatite composite (Cerament G, FDA De Novo 2022) are the two main products; S53P4 bioactive glass is a non-antibiotic antibacterial alternative with European evidence. Upper-extremity cases are a minority of the published series, which are dominated by tibia, femur and calcaneus.
autograft_standard: Staged: antibiotic PMMA beads or spacer, then autogenous cancellous graft (Masquelet induced membrane for segmental defects) once infection is controlled. The single-stage biocomposite protocol (McNally 2016, PMID:27587534) is the challenger.
volume_note: No upper-extremity-specific US volume. In the single-stage Cerament G series the 105 infected bones were predominantly lower limb (McNally 2016); the S53P4 multinational registry was mainly tibia, femur and calcaneus (Lindfors 2017, PMID:28050878). Hand and forearm osteomyelitis is uncommon and usually post-traumatic or diabetic.

name: Clavicle fracture and nonunion

classifications.name: Allman (in words)
classifications.summary: Group I middle third, Group II lateral third, Group III medial third.

classifications.name: Robinson / Edinburgh (in words)
classifications.summary: Type 1 medial fifth, Type 2 diaphyseal (2A undisplaced, 2B displaced; B1 simple/wedge, B2 comminuted/segmental), Type 3 lateral fifth; displacement and comminution drive nonunion risk.

why_biologic: Acute fractures use no biologic. Nonunion revision (plate with or without graft) is where cancellous autograft, DBM or a cellular allograft is used; bone graft lowered delayed union (0.6% vs 3.6%) but was associated with higher complication and reoperation rates in pooled nonunion series (Yetter 2023, PMID:36722838).
autograft_standard: Compression plating with local or iliac crest cancellous autograft for atrophic nonunion; 95% union after primary nonunion surgery across 53 studies, 1,258 nonunions.
volume_note: Karl 2015 (PMID:25714441): 5.8 clavicle fractures per 10,000 persons per year (extrapolated ~179,000/yr). Nonoperative nonunion prevalence 6.2% overall and 4.5% for diaphyseal fractures (Robinson 2004, n=868, PMID:15252081); 13.3% for displaced midshaft fractures in adults, with smoking the strongest risk factor (Murray 2013, n=941, PMID:23824382).

name: Distal humerus fracture and supracondylar nonunion

classifications.name: AO/OTA 13
classifications.summary: 13-A extra-articular, 13-B partial articular (lateral/medial condyle, coronal shear capitellum/trochlea), 13-C complete articular with metaphyseal and articular comminution subtypes.

why_biologic: Rarely used acutely; dual-plate fixation without graft is standard. Supracondylar nonunion revision uses autogenous cancellous graft with rigid fixation; DBM or BMP is occasionally added off-label. Total elbow arthroplasty is the fallback in poor bone.
autograft_standard: Iliac crest cancellous autograft with revision ORIF; pooled ORIF success 90% vs 74% for TEA in nonunion series (Vicenti 2025, PMID:40690057).
volume_note: Distal humeral fractures are ~1% of all fractures (Vicenti 2025, PMID:40690057); Karl 2015 lists distal humerus among the less common adult upper-extremity fractures. No US biologic-use volume exists.

name: Anterior glenoid bone loss in recurrent instability (bone block)

classifications.name: Glenoid bone loss threshold (in words)
classifications.summary: Percent loss of the inferior glenoid circle on en-face CT; 'critical' loss commonly cited at 20-25% and 'subcritical' at 13.5-20%, with bipolar (Hill-Sachs on-track/off-track) assessment.

why_biologic: Adjacent to trauma but a real allograft market: when glenoid bone loss exceeds the subcritical threshold, soft-tissue Bankart repair fails and the surgeon restores the arc with a bone block. Latarjet (coracoid autograft transfer) is the dominant procedure; fresh distal tibia allograft (DTA) is the main allograft alternative because its curvature and dense cartilage match the glenoid, with iliac crest autograft (Eden-Hybbinette) and femoral head allograft as other options.
autograft_standard: Latarjet coracoid transfer: no donor-site harvest beyond the coracoid, but graft resorption, screw problems and nonanatomic reconstruction; iliac crest autograft carries donor-site morbidity.
volume_note: No national US Latarjet count found. New York State Latarjet volume rose 950% from 2003 to 2014 (12 to 126 procedures/yr) while open Bankart fell 77% (Paoli 2018, PMID:29570763). DTA remains a small share; the first RCT vs Latarjet (NCT05658289, n=68, Nova Scotia) is due to complete primary follow-up in 2026.

name: Humeral shaft fracture (acute)

classifications.name: AO/OTA 12
classifications.summary: 12-A simple (spiral, oblique, transverse), 12-B wedge, 12-C multifragmentary; sub-coded by level (proximal, middle, distal third).

why_biologic: Essentially none in the acute setting. Functional bracing or plate/nail fixation without graft is standard; the biologic question only arises if the fracture fails to unite. Included so the atlas is honest that this is a no-biologic segment.
autograft_standard: Not applicable acutely. Anderson-style compression plating with autograft reserved for segmental bone loss.
volume_note: Humeral shaft fractures are a minority of the ~370,000 annual US humerus-fracture ED visits (Kim 2012, PMID:22162357). Nonoperative treatment carries a pooled nonunion rate of 17.6% vs 6.3% with fixation (Sargeant 2020, PMID:32788928); a single-center series found 17% nonunion with bracing, worst in proximal-third fractures (Ali 2015, PMID:25088479). Operative treatment reduced nonunion (OR 0.30) across 4 RCTs and 13 cohorts (Li 2024, PMID:39165869).

name: Humeral shaft nonunion

classifications.name: Weber-Cech (in words)
classifications.summary: Hypertrophic (viable, needs stability) vs atrophic/oligotrophic (biologically inert, needs stability plus graft); infected nonunion handled separately.

why_biologic: The classic upper-extremity biologics case: atrophic nonunion after bracing or failed nailing is revised with compression plating plus autogenous cancellous or structural graft. DBM, rhBMP-2 (Infuse, off-label), rhBMP-7 (historically), cellular allograft and BMAC have all been used as extenders or substitutes, mostly without comparative evidence. Oliver 2021 (PMID:34267148) showed 93% union with plate alone and only 13% grafted, which is the strongest argument that biologics are not routinely needed.
autograft_standard: Compression plate plus iliac crest cancellous autograft: 98% union in pooled series (Peters 2015 systematic review, n=672 plated with autograft, PMID:26499226). Downsides are donor-site pain, hematoma and added operative time; Oliver 2021 argues grafting is not routinely required.
volume_note: No US volume figure found. France records fewer than 700 aseptic humeral shaft nonunions per year (Begue 2023, PMID:36942794); scaling by population suggests low thousands per year in the US (atlas extrapolation, unverified). Medicare 5% sample: 2.5% of all fractures coded as nonunion (Zura 2017, PMID:27836732).

name: Proximal humerus fracture, locked plating with augmentation

classifications.name: Neer (in words)
classifications.summary: Counts displaced parts (head, shaft, greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity); 2-, 3- and 4-part fractures, with fracture-dislocation and head-split variants. Displacement threshold 1 cm or 45 degrees. Interobserver reliability is poor (Pandey 2023, PMID:37636006).

classifications.name: AO/OTA 11
classifications.summary: 11-A extra-articular unifocal, 11-B extra-articular bifocal, 11-C articular/anatomic neck. Medial hinge integrity and metaphyseal comminution drive the decision to augment.

why_biologic: Locked plates fail by varus collapse and screw cut-out, especially in osteoporotic bone with medial comminution; the biologic (an endosteal fibular strut allograft, a calcium phosphate or calcium sulfate/HA void filler, or cancellous chips) is used to restore medial column support and fill the metaphyseal void so screws do not settle. Most proximal humerus fractures are treated nonoperatively and most ORIFs still use no augmentation.
autograft_standard: No true autograft standard here; tricortical iliac crest or vascularized pectoralis-pedicle graft is used by some for 4-part fractures (Karslioglu 2024 RCT, PMID:37625692) but the practical comparator is plate alone, with hemiarthroplasty or reverse arthroplasty as the alternative for unreconstructable fractures.
volume_note: US ED visits for humerus fractures were ~370,000 in 2008, half of them proximal (Kim 2012, PMID:22162357). Karl 2015 (PMID:25714441) found 6.0 proximal humerus fractures per 10,000 persons per year in an 8-state all-payer sample (extrapolated ~185,000/yr). Surgically treated volume rose 13% from 2010-2019; ORIF remained the most common surgery while reverse arthroplasty volume rose >300% (Cooke 2024, PMID:38706683). Nonunion after ORIF is uncommon; mechanical failure (settling, screw penetration, varus collapse) is the dominant complication (Gardner 2007, PMID:17473755).

name: Rotator cuff repair augmentation (adjacent soft-tissue biologics)

classifications.name: Tear size (in words)
classifications.summary: Partial-thickness (articular, bursal, intrasubstance; grade by percent thickness), full-thickness small <1 cm, medium 1-3 cm, large 3-5 cm, massive >5 cm or two or more tendons; retear graded on MRI by Sugaya type IV-V.

why_biologic: One-paragraph adjacent note, not a bone biologic: the same sports-medicine and extremities reps who carry bone void fillers also sell onlay patches that are placed over the repaired tendon to thicken it and lower retear. Options are a bioinductive bovine collagen implant (Regeneten, Smith+Nephew, 510(k) K222501/K242631), acellular human dermal allograft (GraftJacket, ArthroFlex, 361 HCT/Ps) and an interpositional nanofiber wick (Rotium, Atreon/Nanofiber Solutions, K250021). Evidence is mostly industry-sponsored single-arm cohorts; the one sponsor-run RCT in large/massive tears (NCT04450342, n=119) was terminated early and its posted 6-month retear rates were 57.1% augmented vs 50.0% control, which cuts against the marketing. A small investigator RCT of dermal allograft in 2-tendon tears >3 cm (Barber 2012, n=42, PMID:21978432) favored augmentation.
autograft_standard: Not applicable; primary double-row repair without augmentation is the comparator. Autologous options (biceps tendon autograft, fascia lata) exist but are not commercial products.
volume_note: US rotator cuff repair volume rose 141% from 1996 to 2006 with the shift to ambulatory surgery (Colvin 2012, PMID:22298054); New York State volume rose from 6,656 to 10,128 per year between 1997 and 2002 with ambulatory share reaching 82% (Sherman 2008, PMID:18264848). This is a far larger procedure base than any upper-extremity bone-biologic indication.

name: Burr hole and craniotomy gap fill

classifications.name: Defect type
classifications.summary: Burr holes (about 14 mm) from trephination, chronic subdural hematoma drainage or craniotomy, and the contiguous kerf gap left after a craniotomy bone flap is replaced. All US cements are labeled for burr holes, contiguous craniotomy cuts and other cranial defects not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure, usually with a 25 cm2 ceiling (4 cm2 for Stryker DirectInject).

why_biologic: Cosmetic and protective fill of the hole or gap so the scalp does not dimple; the material is a resorbable or non-resorbable osteoconductive plug or paste. Autologous bone dust packed into burr holes resorbs: one comparative series found partial or complete resorption at one year in every bone-dust hole and a visible contour defect in 60 percent, against stable hydroxyapatite plugs.
autograft_standard: Autologous bone dust from the craniotomy, or leaving the hole open under a titanium burr-hole cover (hardware). Many centers use nothing. Burr hole covers and plates are hardware.
volume_note: No public count of US burr holes or craniotomies with gap fill exists. Craniotomy volume is the denominator; the NIS cranioplasty counts above are a lower bound for cranial closure procedures.
hardware_note: Titanium burr-hole covers and craniotomy fixation plates (Stryker Universal Neuro, DePuy Synthes MatrixNEURO, KLS Martin, Zimmer Biomet) are the hardware alternative. RevBio TETRANITE bone adhesive for cranial flap fixation is in a 20-patient FDA-approved first-in-human study (IDE 2023, NIH SBIR 2024); Abyrx has registered NCT07103330 (n=100, start 2026) for cranial flap fixation with Montage Flowable paste, an unlabeled use.

name: Cranioplasty: cranial defect reconstruction after decompressive craniectomy or tumor resection

classifications.name: Cranial defect size (labeling and literature convention)
classifications.summary: Small defects up to 25 cm2 are the labeled ceiling for every US calcium phosphate and HA cranial cement and for PCL scaffolds; defects larger than 25 cm2 (a typical hemicraniectomy flap is 80 to 150 cm2) are reconstructed with the banked autologous flap or a custom alloplastic implant. CPT splits cranioplasty at 5 cm diameter (62140 up to 5 cm, 62141 over 5 cm).

classifications.name: Defect etiology
classifications.summary: Post-decompressive craniectomy (trauma, malignant stroke, hemorrhage), post-tumor resection, infected or resorbed prior flap, congenital or post-craniofacial surgery contour defect. Trauma etiology and younger age raise resorption risk of autologous flaps.

classifications.name: Timing of cranioplasty
classifications.summary: Ultra-early (30 to 45 days), intermediate (45 to 70 days), early (80 to 100 days) and delayed (120 to 180 days) after craniectomy; a 2026 meta-analysis of 55 studies found better functional recovery with cranioplasty within 100 days and no increase in complications.

why_biologic: Biologics here are the self-setting calcium phosphate and hydroxyapatite cements, beta-TCP, bioactive glass and DBM used to fill small defects or restore contour; they are osteoconductive void fillers, not structural. They do not compete with the autologous flap for large defects; the competition for large defects is custom PEEK, titanium or PMMA implants (hardware, see adjacent note).
autograft_standard: Reimplantation of the patient's own bone flap, banked by cryopreservation or in a subcutaneous abdominal pocket, is the benchmark. Its failure modes are aseptic bone flap resorption (pooled 15 to 20 percent in adults, around 40 percent for banked flaps in children) and infection (around 7 percent), which together drive reoperation odds about 1.9 times those of synthetic implants. Cryopreservation and subcutaneous storage give similar infection and resorption rates. Split calvarial graft is the autograft for smaller defects and for children.
volume_note: No single US annual cranioplasty count is published. National Inpatient Sample series report 49,305 weighted adult cranioplasty encounters for 2012 to 2014 (about 16,000 per year; PMID 33055559) and 105,714 adult cranioplasty admissions for 2002 to 2017 (about 6,600 per year; PMID 35526812); the two code definitions differ, so the app should show the range and the sources. Upstream, decompressive craniectomy for stroke was performed in 124,718 NIS patients over 2006 to 2016 (PMID 32173551) and 6.8 percent (23,743 of 349,164) of severe TBI admissions had a craniectomy over 2004 to 2014 (PMID 36202343).
hardware_note: Custom patient-specific cranial implants are hardware, cleared under product codes GXN and GWO (21 CFR 882.5330 and 882.5320): Stryker PEEK Customized Cranial Implant (K203055, 2021) and Cranial iD, DePuy Synthes Patient Specific Implants (K243715, 2025) and TRUMATCH CMF, KLS Martin IPS-Ti and IPS-PEEK (consolidated MR-conditional clearance K252573, 2025), Oxford Performance Materials OsteoFab PEKK (K180064, 2018), Longeviti ClearFit sonolucent PMMA (K203349, K231920, K260709), Kelyniam, 3D Systems VSP PEEK (K231834), Fin-Ceramica CustomizedBone porous HA (K240567), OssDsign Cranial PSI (K161090). A 2025 systematic review of 3,260 custom heterologous cranioplasties reported infection and explantation of 8.2 and 3.7 percent for titanium, 6.7 and 5.3 percent for porous hydroxyapatite, 14.9 and 6.1 percent for PMMA and 11.1 and 3.8 percent for PEEK (PMID 40971008).

name: Craniosynostosis and pediatric cranial vault reconstruction (primary remodeling and secondary contour cranioplasty)

classifications.name: Suture involved
classifications.summary: Sagittal (scaphocephaly), metopic (trigonocephaly), unicoronal (anterior plagiocephaly), bicoronal (brachycephaly), lambdoid (posterior plagiocephaly); single-suture nonsyndromic versus multisuture syndromic (Apert, Crouzon, Pfeiffer, Saethre-Chotzen, Muenke).

classifications.name: Procedure
classifications.summary: Endoscopic strip craniectomy with helmet (under about 6 months), open cranial vault remodeling or fronto-orbital advancement (6 to 12 months), posterior vault distraction; secondary contour cranioplasty in adolescence for residual temporal or supraorbital hollowing after fronto-orbital advancement (reported in up to 55 to 75 percent, with up to 20 percent needing correction).

why_biologic: In primary surgery the vault is reshaped with the child's own bone; bone gaps left after remodeling are usually left to the osteogenic dura in infants, with DBM or particulate bone used to bridge gaps in older children or large defects. In secondary contour cranioplasty, hydroxyapatite and carbonated calcium phosphate cements are onlayed over intact cranium; this is an off-label-adjacent use (cements are labeled for contour restoration up to 25 cm2) with infection and removal rates of 5 to 10 percent and higher when large volumes are used.
autograft_standard: Autologous calvarial bone (split or particulate) is the standard; children under about 2 years lack a diploic space for split grafts, which is why DBM and resorbable mesh bilaminate was developed for large defects. Resorbable fixation (DePuy Synthes RapidSorb, KLS Martin Resorb-x, Stryker Delta, Zimmer Biomet LactoSorb) is hardware with a 7.9 percent wound complication rate in a 325-patient series.
volume_note: Kids' Inpatient Database: 3,426 craniosynostosis repairs in the four sampled years 1997, 2000, 2003 and 2006 (PMID 23030675); 2012 KID counts about 1,600 to 1,800 repairs in infants under 12 months; NSQIP-Pediatric captured 11,279 repairs over 2012 to 2021 (PMID 38940557). Birth prevalence is about 1 in 2,000 to 2,500 live births (literature convention; no single CDC national estimate located).

name: Lateral skull base defect repair (translabyrinthine, retrosigmoid, temporal bone) and frontal sinus obliteration

classifications.name: Approach-defined defects
classifications.summary: Translabyrinthine and retrosigmoid craniectomy defects after vestibular schwannoma or other cerebellopontine angle surgery; mastoid and temporal bone defects; frontal sinus obliteration after osteoplastic flap for chronic frontal sinusitis or fracture.

why_biologic: Hydroxyapatite cement is used to seal air-cell tracts and reconstruct the craniectomy so cerebrospinal fluid cannot leak and the postauricular contour is restored; this is the one cranial application where cement has comparative data showing lower CSF leak and pseudomeningocele odds than fat graft or no reconstruction. Bioactive glass S53P4 granules (Bonalive) are used to obliterate the frontal sinus because they are osteoconductive and bacteriostatic.
autograft_standard: Abdominal fat graft for translabyrinthine closure and autologous bone or fat for frontal sinus obliteration; fat alone has historically carried about 12 percent CSF leak after translabyrinthine resection. HA cement should not touch sinus mucosa or be used to obliterate an infected mastoid cavity (three of three mastoid obliterations failed in one pediatric series).
volume_note: No US volume count found for translabyrinthine or retrosigmoid craniectomy reconstruction or frontal sinus obliteration (PubMed searched 2026-10-22).

name: Alveolar cleft bone grafting (secondary alveolar bone graft)

classifications.name: Veau classification of cleft palate
classifications.summary: Veau I: cleft of the soft palate only. Veau II: cleft of the soft and hard palate up to the incisive foramen. Veau III: complete unilateral cleft of the soft and hard palate and the alveolus and lip. Veau IV: complete bilateral cleft of lip, alveolus and palate. The alveolar cleft is present in Veau III and IV and in isolated cleft lip and alveolus.

classifications.name: Timing of alveolar grafting
classifications.summary: Primary (under 2 years, with lip repair; largely abandoned), secondary (mixed dentition, 6 to 11 years, before canine eruption; the standard), late secondary or tertiary (after canine eruption, worse outcomes).

classifications.name: Outcome scales
